that everyone sees he has stirred up the hatred of many.
Those who are of a very sharp judgment in weighing the speeches of men should see, read, and carefully investigate this argument to see if anything offends them. If something displeases them, let them not immediately knit their brows or curl their lips. Let them place their trust in the judgment of the more learned, who will bring forth none but a true verdict concerning my Charles. For who, I ask, does not see how brilliantly he treats this most arduous argument? The weight of almost every word is balanced by the corresponding words (which is rare among theologians), and the subject matter is not disparate from the sentiments. And to sum up, they are seen to be so fitting that he seems to excel not only modern writers but even <note>Saint</note> Jerome himself, if I dare say so. For if he is sparing of words above all else, he is nevertheless rich in sentiments: he is not barren, nor does he waste away with sterility. If you seek medicinal sweetness and delight, no one more perfectly soothes the ears, penetrates the soul more vividly, or urges more intensely. To these ends, therefore, most holy pastor, so that the excellence of your magnificence might be more nobly elevated, I have labored zealously to send this argument (which it does not disgrace any prelate to know) to your Highness. I have imitated certain men (whose names have slipped my memory through carelessness) who never greet their King without a gift. It was my intention to suppress the encomiums of your virtues and rare happiness, lest I appear a vain flatterer; for I know that you are no more moved by praises than a blind man is by painted tablets. Although you may be considered a child of birth or fortune (I pass over other gifts of the body), this can still be truthfully and ingenuously said of you, which was taken from that Cato of Utica: You are the true image of virtue.

Therefore, for these reasons, most holy pastor, I have labored more diligently so that the excellence of your magnificence might be more nobly elevated. I have striven to send this argument—which it does not disgrace any prelate to know—to your Highness. I have imitated certain men (whose names have slipped my mind due to negligence) who never greet their King without a gift. It was my intention to suppress the encomiums of your virtues and rare happiness, lest I appear a boastful flatterer. For I know that you are no more moved by praises than a bleary-eyed man is by painted tablets. Although you may be considered a product of either birth or fortune (I pass over other gifts of the body), nevertheless, that which was borrowed from Cato the Younger <note>original: "Cato Uticensis"</note> can be frankly said of you: You are the true image of virtue <note>original: "virtutis ymago"</note>.

if fiery meteors were to be formed in this way, it would be necessary for another fiery meteor to arise from the smoke of a falling star, and from the smoke of that, yet another, and so on to infinity, a condition which nature detests. Furthermore, an effect is never more noble than its cause. The author is also inconsistent in claiming that windy meteors arise from vapor and smoke. It is more accurate to say that these originate from the air, or from a spirit trapped within the earth that has arisen from the air. The qualities of vapor and smoke do not possess the same affinity with the qualities of windy meteors as the air does. He also seems to have erred in stating that springs arise from airy atoms trapped and condensed within the earth, a claim we deny entirely. Regarding the first point, that springs are formed from atoms, his opinion is absurd; consider how many atoms would be required for a single, entire spring, when even one tiny drop consists of many myriads of atoms. Moreover, his claim that springs arise from condensed airy atoms contradicts the opinion of the <term>Physicorum</term> <gloss>natural philosophers</gloss>, who maintain that the elements do not transmute into one another, such that water is made from air. Furthermore, the effect is of the same nature as the cause; the effect is water, therefore the cause must also be water. Although a certain spring may sometimes appear to arise anew, it does not truly originate; rather, it is manifested after being concealed. More could be said about this at another time.

§ 15. It remains for us to say a few words about corruption, by which these minimal bodies, once formed, each tend toward their own species. When all bodies decay, they emit much vapor or smoke, which are nothing other than contiguous bodies composed of many myriads of atoms. These do not vanish into nothingness, but are separated in an invisible state, and each returns to its own species. We provide the example of fire: if you sprinkle water on embers, the fire vanishes. It would be wrong to say that an annihilation of the fire has occurred, or that it has perished; rather, it is merely concealed by an enemy <note>meaning the water</note> that denies it the ventilation it requires. Consider further the combustion of a certain body, in which the conversion of the body into fire does not occur, but rather its resolution into its minimal parts, which, when dispersed and dissolved, can no longer be seen, even though they were visible when conjoined. If one asks where these minimal parts go upon corruption, we answer that they go into a vacuum to fill it, for a vacuum does not exist in nature because nature loves unity. There are other functions that these minimal parts of nature perform which are worthy of dissertation.

<summary>The author critiques the theories regarding the formation of meteors and springs from vapor and atoms, arguing instead for the constancy of elements and the resolution of decaying bodies into their constituent parts rather than their annihilation.</summary>
<keywords>meteors, atoms, natural philosophy, corruption, vacuum, elements, springs, transmutation</keywords>

if fiery meteors were to be formed, it would be necessary for another fiery meteor to arise from the smoke of a falling star, and from the smoke of this one yet another, and so on to infinity, which nature abhors. Furthermore, an effect is never nobler than its own cause. Nor is the author consistent here, as he says that windy meteors <note>referring to meteorological phenomena involving air movement</note> arise from vapor and smoke. Yet it would be better and more accurate to say that these things are made by air, or by the spirit enclosed within the earth which originates from the air. For the qualities of vapor and smoke do not have the same affinity with the qualities of windy meteors as air does. He also seems to have erred in this, when he posits that springs arise from airy atoms enclosed and condensed within the earth, which we deny entirely. Regarding the first point, namely that springs are made of atoms, his opinion is absurd; for how many atoms would be required for a whole spring, given that a single drop consists of many myriads of atoms? Moreover, his claim that springs are made from condensed airy atoms conflicts with the opinion of natural philosophers, who maintain that the elements are not transmuted, such that water is made from air. Furthermore, the effect is of the same nature as the cause; the effect is water, therefore the cause must also be water. Even if a certain spring sometimes appears to arise anew, it does not truly emerge as something new, but rather what was hidden is made manifest. More could be said on these matters at another time.

§ 15. It remains for us to bring forward a few points regarding corruption, by which these smallest bodies, once acted upon, each tend toward their own species. When all bodies rot, they emit much vapor or smoke, which are nothing other than contiguous bodies composed of many myriads of atoms. These do not vanish into nothingness, but are separated under an invisible form, and each returns to its own species. We provide the example of fire for this: if you sprinkle water on embers, the fire vanishes; it would be incorrect to say that this is an annihilation of fire, or that it perishes, but rather it is merely hidden by an enemy that denies it the necessary ventilation. Consider further the combustion of a body, in which the body is not converted into fire, but is resolved into its smallest parts, which are then scattered and dissolved so that they can no longer be seen, whereas they could be seen when conjoined. If one asks where these smallest parts go when corruption occurs, we answer: into a vacuum, so that they may fill it. For a vacuum does not exist in nature, as nature loves unity. There would be other things which these smallest parts of nature perform that are worthy of dissertation.

<summary>The author critiques theories regarding the formation of meteorological phenomena and the nature of springs, arguing against the transmutation of elements and asserting that corruption involves the resolution of bodies into their constituent atoms rather than annihilation, all while maintaining that nature abhors a vacuum.</summary>
<keywords>Meteors, Atoms, Corruption, Springs, Vacuum, Natural Philosophy, Elements</keywords>

not just in words, but in reality, for otherwise the competition of creditors <note>original: "concursus"</note> appears simulated and fraudulent. Salgado, in the aforementioned chapter 1, number 17 and following. The same was established in the Provincial Decree of the March of Brandenburg <note>original: "Recessu Provinciali Marchico"</note> of the year 1653, paragraph 33, which states: rather, the overburdened debtors <note>original: "oberati Debitores"</note> are to be removed from their estates, and the entire proceeds are to be sequestered for the benefit of the creditors, et cetera. Although a debtor is sometimes accustomed to being retained on the estate as a manager <note>original: "conductor"</note> for a fixed rent to be paid, sometimes he is also retained as an administrator <note>original: "curator"</note>, subject to rendering accounts.

**CESSION)** This differs from the process of competition. If someone wishes to make a cession of goods, there is a need for the harassment of creditors, which is not the case in a competition. A cession of goods can take place regarding certain creditors, whereas a competition applies to all. Hence, in a cession, an edictal citation is not precisely necessary; see Salgado, part 1, chapter 1, number 46 and following. However, when a competition has been initiated, a cession of goods must always follow (regarding which our author speaks here), but not vice versa.

**CURATOR)** This applies if it has been so decided by the creditors, at whose risk the matter is conducted. Indeed, the administration is sometimes even entrusted to the widow of the deceased, so that she may render accounts to the creditors; but this is dangerous, since the debtor and his widow alike are more concerned with their own advantage than with that of the creditors, so that it is wiser to appoint another curator. Mevius, on the Law of Lübeck, book 3, title 1, article 10, number 32 and following. See below, paragraph XI.

->§. VII.<-

33. From this, one may conclude that not all Stoics approved of suicide <note>original: "propricidium"</note> without distinction. Furthermore, even if this were granted, it does not follow that all legal scholars <term>Jurisconsultos</term> <gloss>jurists/legal experts</gloss> were Stoics. And even if this were conceded, it still does not follow that they approved of <term>αυτοχειριαν</term> <gloss>self-slaughter/suicide</gloss>. For by the same reasoning, we could conclude that the remaining dogmas of the Stoics were also adopted by the legal scholars, for instance, that sins are equal, that the wise man does not lie, and so forth. There is also no logical consequence that because the legal scholars were Stoics and approved of <term>αυτοχειριαν</term> <gloss>self-slaughter</gloss>, therefore it is permitted under civil law. This argument would only proceed if our law were to be judged by the initial composition of the legal scholars and not by the authority of the Prince Justinian, a Christian learned in the sacred scriptures. And to the cited laws, beyond the answer provided by Heigius, it may be said that the texts speak only of the confiscation of goods, by which one who has committed <term>αυτοχειριᾳ</term> <gloss>self-slaughter</gloss> is not to be affected, unless he has laid violent hands upon himself out of fear of punishment. From this, however, it does not follow that therefore <term>αυτοχειρια</term> <gloss>self-slaughter</gloss> is lawful by right, nor that it goes entirely unpunished. For this consequence is refuted by law 2 of the Code, where the fiscal cause is mentioned, where the confiscation of goods is set against the penalty of death, and where <term>αυτοχειρια</term> <gloss>self-slaughter</gloss> is called a crime.

# CHAPTER II.

A person is punished with death for a crime by one who is established in a public office. This is required by divine justice, the safety of the republic, and for the sake of the offenders themselves. For God does not wish to absolve the wicked and in no way justify the guilty, but His justice requires that it go well for the good and ill for the evil. Hence David says in Psalm 101, *In the morning I will immediately destroy all the wicked in the land, that I may cut off from the city of God all those who do iniquity.* The safety of the Republic demands this. For it is testified in Novella 77, chapter 1, at the beginning, that whole cities have perished on account of crimes. And if crimes are left unpunished, peace and tranquility are driven away. For that to be preserved, the magistrate ought to act with solicitude so that the Republic may be rid of evil men, and that those who commit sacrilege, robbers, kidnappers, and thieves may be punished in the due manner, as Ulpian teaches in law 13 of the Digest concerning the duty of a governor. For to these, they ought to show themselves terrible so that, by degrees, the punishment may keep all others safe. The cause of the offenders themselves likewise demands this. For punishments are established for their reformation, as seen in law 20 concerning punishments, and so that those who have sown iniquity may reap trouble, according to Proverbs 22, verse 8.

33. From this it can be gathered that not all Stoics indiscriminately approved of self-killing <note>original: "propricidium"</note>. Furthermore, even if this were granted, it does not follow from it that all legal experts <term>Jurisconsultos</term> <gloss>Roman legal scholars/jurists</gloss> were Stoics. And if this were also granted, it still does not follow that they approved of <term>αυτοχειριαν</term> <gloss>self-slaughter/suicide</gloss>. For by the same reasoning, we could conclude that the remaining Stoic dogmas were also accepted by legal experts, for instance, that sins are equal, that the wise man does not lie, and so forth. For this would only hold if our law were to be judged by the original drafting of the legal experts, and not by the authority of the Prince Justinian, who was a Christian and instructed in the Holy Scriptures. ## 1. Origins of the Work

Our text has long been considered a somewhat belated countermeasure of Catholic controversial theology against the publication of Melanchthon’s *Loci communes* <gloss>Common Places</gloss>. As early as one year after the appearance of the *Enchiridion* <gloss>Handbook</gloss>, Zwingli wrote to Vadian: "Eccius <note>Eck</note> has explained certain common places, imitating Melanchthon, as I believe..."¹. This view was apparently common in the 16th century². It is found in the classic 19th-century works on Catholic controversial theology³, and it is considered established to this day⁴. However, if Melanchthon was the model, the practical initiative, as Eck himself relates, came from the legate Lorenzo Campeggio⁵.

That is not the whole story, however. Eck had been considering the idea of a comprehensive refutation, not limited to individual topics or individual works of Reformation theology, since 1523. We can follow the emergence of such a plan in his work with some precision.

It is well known that in 1520, Eck was very actively involved in Rome in the drafting of the bull of excommunication *Exsurge Domine* <gloss>Arise, O Lord</gloss>, especially, it seems, in the selection of Lutheran writings that had not been considered in the *Condemnationes* <gloss>Condemnations</gloss> of Cologne and Louvain⁶. At the same time, he had begun to participate very actively in that production of polemical writings which Hubert Jedin⁷ has described as "the high tide of publicism."

Few of the writings published before 1523 deal with a large number of different controversial issues. In Fabri’s *Malleus* <gloss>Hammer</gloss>, for instance, many are treated only tangentially, and the work focuses largely on the questions of Church and authority that were paramount for the Roman Catholic interlocutor. # NOTES

*Fam. i. 4 [9 August 1333]*

**Page 1.** Giovanni Colonna was the second son of Stefano, the head of the house of Colonna at this time. Petrarch was on a footing of intimate friendship with several members of this family. There are sixteen letters addressed to Giovanni, as well as several metrical epistles and the sonnet, *Rime* cclxvi. In *Sen.* xvi. 1 Petrarch gives an account of his friendship with the younger brother Giacomo; while both were students at the University of Bologna they had been attracted to one another, but it was not until after Petrarch’s return to Avignon in April 1326 that they became friends. (F. Lo Parco has tried to show in *Errors . . . in the biography of Petrarch* <note>original: "Errori . . . nella biogr. del P."</note>, ‘Journal of Italian Literary History’ <note>original: "Giorn. stor. d. lett. ital."</note>, xlviii, 1906, pp. 37-69, that Petrarch returned to Avignon at the end of 1325, and as a result puts back by a year the date of a number of the earlier letters. But the case against the traditional date, 1326, is not proved. See also P. de Nolhac, *Petrarch in Bologna in the time of Azzo Visconti* <note>original: "P. à Bologne au temps d’Azzo Visconti"</note>, in ‘Petrarch and Lombardy’ <note>original: "P. e la Lombardia"</note>, Milan, 1904, pp. 87-93.) Giacomo, now Bishop of Lombez, took Petrarch with him to his see in Gascony (on this journey see F. Lo Parco, *Petrarch and Giacomo Colonna in Toulouse* <note>original: "Il P. e Giacomo Colonna a Tolosa"</note>, in ‘Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Archaeology . . . in Naples’ <note>original: "Mem. d. R. Accad. di archeol. . . . in Napoli"</note>, 1911, pt. 2, p. 229 seq.), and on their return to Avignon in 1330 introduced him to his brother the Cardinal. From 1330-7 Petrarch was living in the Cardinal’s house at Avignon, and was probably to some extent dependent on him. It was not until 1335 that he received his first Church preferment, a canonry at Lombez. The Cardinal probably paid the expenses of the journey which this letter describes, and we shall hear of Petrarch’s securing his consent for his visit to Rome in 1337. Giovanni was created a Cardinal by Pope John XXII in 1327 before he had reached the age of thirty. For other details of Petrarch’s relations with the family see *Fam.* iv. 6, v. 3, and viii. 1.

In *Sen.* xvi. 1 Petrarch gives an account of his friendship with the younger brother Giacomo; while both were students at the University of Bologna they had been attracted to one another, but it was not until after Petrarch’s return to Avignon in April 1326 that they became friends. <note>F. Lo Parco has argued in *Errori . . . nella biogr. del P.* (Giorn. stor. d. lett. ital., xlviii, 1906, pp. 37-69) that Petrarch returned to Avignon at the end of 1325, and consequently dates several early letters a year earlier. ### On Removing Drunkenness.

Because wine is death to the poison of hemlock, it has been imagined and truly discovered that, for others, hemlock is life. Pliny seems to hint at this. Poisons are even prepared for the sake of drinking, with some taking hemlock beforehand so that death might force them to drink. If one has consumed wine too liberally and feels harm to the body, this will disperse the effects for the drinker. Cato teaches that one should eat four or five sprouts of raw cabbage at the beginning and end of a meal, for it settles drunkenness, extinguishes the harm of wine, and restores you as if you had eaten and drunk nothing. The Egyptians used to eat boiled cabbage before every meal, preparing themselves in this way for drinking bouts. Many, in order to be protected from drunkenness, take cabbage seed beforehand. The Sybarites, says Timaeus, protected themselves against drinking by eating cabbage. Alexis writes:

> *Yesterday you drank more than enough: now you feel*
> *A heavy head; this ill must be treated by fasting.*
> *Then someone will give you some boiled*
> *Cabbage.*

Thus also Amphis:

> *There is no remedy more readily available for the drunk,*
> *Than if something troublesome happens*
> *Suddenly, for it dissipates such nonsense*
> *In a wonderful way, so that even the radish is no more*
> *Effective for this purpose.*

Some were accustomed to using an <term>amethystinum vasculum</term> <gloss>a vessel made of amethyst</gloss> before a drinking session, so that they could indulge in wine with impunity, according to Athenaeus. If you wish to inhibit the harm of wine in another way, consume it well-diluted; for those who drink it undiluted feel the drunkenness more quickly than those who drink it straight, as Africanus teaches. Indeed, it is a particular stratagem of Satan to attribute the invention of things to idols and the gods of the nations, or to those men who performed notable work in spreading idolatry. For he took special care, fearing for himself and his kingdom of darkness, that men should not learn anything about the Divine Scriptures, and that nothing should be thought better than the writings of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, or Greeks. Matthaeus Berald, *Chronicles*, book 1, folio 49. From this arises the vanity and uncertainty of ethnic <note>pagan</note> arts and philosophy; for indeed, by the fault of our first parents, we are hindered from enjoying the full light of nature even in these human matters. # Cap. III.
## On the Jurisconsults of Roman Law.

<note>A decorative initial letter A begins the chapter.</note>
Under the Emperor Augustus, there was already at Rome, as Livy speaks (book 3, chapter 34), an immense heap of laws piled one upon another, or, to use the words of Tacitus (Annals, book 3, chapter 25), just as it had previously labored under crimes, so it then labored under laws, because the situation had already reached an infinite multitude and variety of laws. Therefore, just as the forums and courts of that city could no longer be practiced for some time without laborious legal expertise, so too, from such a great number and diversity of laws, the authority of men in that profession grew by a certain necessity not a little, contrary to what had been customary either there until then or elsewhere in the world. Furthermore, who practiced the science of Roman Law before that age must be sought from Pomponius on the Origin of Law. In that age, however, Ateius Capito and Antistius Labeo were of the greatest authority. These two, to use the words of Pomponius, first established, as it were, different sects; for Capito persevered in those things which had been handed down to him, whereas Labeo, because of the quality of his intellect and confidence in his learning—who had also devoted himself to the study of other branches of wisdom—began to innovate many things. It is further clear from Pomponius that both had disciples: Masurius Sabinus to Capito, and Nerva to Labeo, who even further increased these dissensions, namely in the age of Tiberius, Claudius, and Gaius. §. 2.
1. After St. Martin’s Day <note>November 11th</note>, the field is manured if the weather permits; the manure is spread very evenly and plowed under to a depth of 8 inches.

In this fresh furrow, one quarter pound of each type of seed is sown per <term>Morgen</term> <gloss>a traditional unit of land area, roughly equivalent to an acre</gloss>, totaling 15 pounds for 4 <term>Morgen</term>, mixed with 8 bushels of soil. This is done during calm weather and diligently harrowed (raked) in, after which the field remains in this state throughout the winter.

§. 3.
In the spring, this seed germinates seven to eight weeks earlier because other people cannot cultivate their fields as early due to snow and wet conditions.

§. 4.
Between Easter and Pentecost, the weeds are carefully removed. This requires sensible people who must know these plant species so they do not pull them out as weeds.

§. 5.

8. Not a few have merely rewritten their own material and placed their names under someone else's work; thus, everything they produced is merely something rearranged. This is true whether the Latins translated it from the Greek, or whether Greeks and Latins alike copied from one another.

<margin>Several notable examples of how the ancients stole work from one another.</margin>

Thus, Justinus borrowed all his material from Trogus Pompeius, and Julius Solinus copied Pliny in a certain way. Likewise, Lucian and Apuleius enriched themselves with Lucius of Patrae <note>original: "Lucio Pratense"</note>; both lived at the same time and both copied the same book, inserting it into their famous books, one calling his *Lucius* and the other his *The Golden Ass*. In the same manner, Simocatta dealt with the Nile in his book using Diodorus Siculus. This can be seen in the work attributed to Heraclitus and translated by Jungermann. Thus, Eratosthenes completely rewrote Timotheus on the Islands, to such an extent that he did not even write a different preface but kept the previous one. Strabo recounts similar things regarding Eudorus and Ariston in a book that also bears the title *On the Nile*. Clement of Alexandria recorded many such examples among the Greeks, and Pliny speaks of this quite clearly in his preface, noting that when he compared his authors and read one work alongside another, he found that the successors commonly copied their material word for word from their predecessors, yet never mentioned their books with a single word. Not to mention that the ingenious work of Ovid belongs more to Parthenius of Nicaea <note>original: "Parthemio Chio"</note> than to him, and the highly famous Virgil borrowed all his works from others: the Eclogues or pastoral dialogues from Theocritus; the Georgics, or *On Agriculture*, from Hesiod and Aratus; and the books on Aeneas from Homer. Among these, as Macrobius notes, he took the second book, in which he relates the story of Sinon and the Trojan Horse, word for word from Pisander. Even our own art (of medicine) is not free from this, as Oribasius, Aetius, and Aegineta wrote their works in a certain way from Galen. However, Marcellus Empiricus, who left behind a famous work on medicines, copied it word for word from Scribonius Largus's *On the Composition of Medicines* <note>original: "De compositione medicamentorum"</note>, and did not even leave out his concluding remarks. are not the works, but one should count them as nothing toward salvation. With this example I conclude: What use is it to the pear tree that it bears beautiful, lovely pears? Nothing. Another person comes and takes them, and the tree does not take them back. So too, what use is it to you that you do good works from faith? It is of no use to you; another takes your works, and that is God. A human takes them from the pear tree, for he occupies the place of God on earth in temporal matters; therefore, he is an earthly god. And just as little as the tree enjoys its fruit, so little do you enjoy your works, even though they come from faith in the best possible way. The praise goes to the good pears, not to the tree. Likewise, although his works are of no use to the believer, he does not abandon them, for it is the nature of faith that it is not without fruit, just as a good tree is not without pears. To the same people.
You suffer because you possess lupines, fish, water, and grand delicacies, yet you are full and grumble much. You betray, you tyrannize, you murder, and you commit all such shameful acts that you do, when you ought to be at peace. We, however, keep the peace in all things. Diogenes.

Mnaso.

If any number of given magnitudes are added together, the magnitude composed of them will also be given.

For let any number of given magnitudes, <term>AB</term> and <term>BΓ</term>, be added together. I say that the magnitude <term>AΓ</term>, composed of <term>AB</term> and <term>BΓ</term>, is also given.

Since the magnitude <term>AB</term> is given, it is possible for a magnitude equal to it to be constructed <note>Definition 1</note>. Let it be constructed, and let it be <term>ΔE</term>. Again, since the magnitude <term>BΓ</term> is given, it is possible for a magnitude equal to it to be constructed <note>Definition 1</note>. Let it be constructed, and let it be <term>EZ</term>. Now, since <term>AB</term> equals <term>ΔE</term> and <term>BΓ</term> equals <term>EZ</term>, the whole <term>AΓ</term> will be equal to the whole <term>ΔZ</term> <note>Common Notion 2</note>. Therefore, the magnitude <term>AΓ</term> is given <note>Definition 1</note>, for a magnitude equal to it, <term>ΔZ</term>, has been constructed.

It is to be regretted that Hultsch, the most recent editor of Polybius, should have introduced a new notation, founded on his own theories and those of Nissen with respect to the assignment of the fragments to the several books. Not much textual criticism is attempted in this volume. The text of Hultsch, who has carefully compared the several <term>MSS.</term> <gloss>manuscripts</gloss>, has been taken as a basis. When the text is evidently corrupt and the editors give us a choice of emendations, I have tried to exercise an independent judgment in each case. "Hang them by the testicles." That is to say, as if carrying a sword against you, as Odysseus did to Circe, which is what happened to Odysseus during the time of Phineus at the mouth of Charybdis, from where he removed Circe. Or just as they hanged Melanthius there. "We shall smear." Some say "minthos" is excrement. Others say it is the <term>iunx</term> <gloss>wryneck bird, used in love charms</gloss>, as in the comic usage. Others say it is a flower growing in dung, which goats enjoy. Or otherwise, "minthos" is called the dung of goats. When goats fall into a fit of sneezing, goatherds are accustomed to take their dung and smear it on their nostrils, and in this way stir up a sneeze, and by this method release the ailment. For a sneeze heals the condition. From then, he says that we shall release you, since even goats are released by the dung. Otherwise, "we shall manure." For "minthos" is a flower growing in dung, which goats enjoy. Others say "minthos" is human excrement, which shepherds use when lengthening the sneeze of goats for the pipe. "You, Arisyllos." The Arisyllos is a lewd man. For the <term>Ecclesiazusae</term> <gloss>Assemblywomen (a play by Aristophanes)</gloss> mentions him as an obscene man. "Lapa" [is used] as the Arisyllos who has plucked the ancient [hair]. The poet calls him obscene because, due to his obscenity, he stooped. That is, you see his nature as if Arisyllos is gaping. "Since for a mother, piglets." Instead of "for me." Then they say it is proverbial. For children are accustomed to say, "Since for a mother, piglets." It is said to be proverbial regarding the uneducated. "But come." These are stated lines and six cola. Of which the first and last are catalectic tetrameters, the ones in between are acatalectic trimeters, and under the end are double marks pointing outward, already at the beginning of the colon or toward the end. "While I, going off." They bite from here, as slaves are accustomed to do such things. "In the labor" [refers to] the city or greater care. From the theme of "chewing." In the conjugation, "chewing," as "breaking." "To greet you." A paragraphos [sign] that the actors are entering. The lines are 6 acatalectic iambic trimeters. The last of which: "And I am walking." Directing it toward the [goal]. Chremylus, as if giving rules to Fortune, devises a newer greeting. For "to greet" is old. From where was it in the custom "to greet," which is written in the letters of Dionysius in a single-book scroll? And he says that it was first established by Cleon, writing to the Athenians how he captured Sphacteria. "Cleon to the Council and the people of the Athenians, greetings." He says that even there it is a poetical [phrase], from where the construction is unclear. Indicating from here that those who suddenly and beyond expectation have good fortune become different in their ways and how they move toward arrogance. For to know how to greet is a bad thing. But through the labor which he previously had been accustomed to, just as he said "but very much so," wishing to change the salutations along with the life. He joins the "already" to the "ancient."

Did I not speak correctly, Adeimantus? Yes, he said, but this "correctly" is, like the rest of the speech, to be established: what is the mode of this community? <note>of the waters failing, and the rivers shall dry up. <term>4 Esdras</term> <gloss>a pseudepigraphical book of the Bible</gloss> vi. 24 And the veins of the fountains shall stand. <term>Testament of Levi</term> 4 waters drying up.</note>

**doing righteousness and judgement.** Compare <term>Ezekiel</term> xviii. 5, "the man who shall be righteous, doing judgement and righteousness," and Psalm cxviii. (cxix.) 121, "I have done judgement and righteousness."

**from ruler... to the vilest of the people.** A very probable instance of a Hebrew idiom imperfectly understood: "from their prince to the very least of the people," meaning both their prince and the dregs of the mob. Compare <term>Jonah</term> iii. 5, "from their great ones even to their small ones." Very possibly "even to" should be supplied here; in xviii. 13 it was omitted by manuscript A and by older editors. The idiom in the <term>LXX</term> <gloss>Septuagint</gloss> is generally rendered by "from... and even to" (compare Ex. ix. 25, Josh. vi. 21, 1 Sam. xv. 3).

Geiger, who also explains the difficulty of the passage as due to a misapprehension of the Hebrew preposition <term>min</term> <gloss>from</gloss>, connects "from their ruler" with the previous clause: "None practiced more than their prince."

**22 The king.** The Asmonean Prince, referring to Hyrcanus II or Aristobulus II.

**in disobedience.** Four of the manuscripts give this reading in place of "in truth," which was so unintelligible that Hilgenfeld's conjectural insertion of "not" was accepted by Fritzsche, Wellhausen ("in corruption"), and Pick, while Geiger suggested "in impiety."

"Disobedience" is not found in the <term>LXX</term>, but "to disobey" is not uncommon, e.g., Isaiah i. 23, "your rulers are disobedient" (<term>Symmachus</term> <gloss>a translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek</gloss> "disobedient"), and iii. 8.

<column-break/>

**23** The Psalmist has described, in the most moving terms he can employ, the state of decay into which the Jewish polity had fallen. To his mind there is only one possible remedy for it: the King promised long before, of the true ancient kingly line.

For the wording of the appeal many parallels can be cited. The promise originally made to David is in 2 Samuel vii. 12. In Jeremiah xxx. 9 we have, "I will raise up to them David their king." Compare Ezekiel xxxiv. 23, xxxvii. 25; and, as perhaps the earliest in date, Amos ix. 11, "I will raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen."

**the time which thou knowest.** Compare Zechariah xiv. 7, "that day shall be known to the Lord." A reference to the old promise is indicated.

**24 Gird** occurs once in 2 Maccabees and in Acts xxvii. 17. The usual <term>LXX</term> expression is "gird with strength," Psalm xviii. 38, 43. In Isaiah xi, the Messiah is girded with righteousness and faithfulness.

**break in pieces.** Compare Numbers xxiv. 17, "he shall break in pieces the princes of Moab." The corrupt Sadducean princes are to be cast down.

For God is not ignorant that our fleshy mass, the body—for Er is interpreted as <term>leathery</term> <gloss>or "fleshy"</gloss>—is wicked and a conspirator against the soul, and always dead and deceased. For what else do we do in each of our lives but carry a corpse, while the soul raises this dead body from itself and carries it without toil?

And consider, if you will, the strength of the soul. The most vigorous athlete could not carry his own statue for even a short time, yet the soul often carries the human statue for up to a hundred years without tiring. For God did not kill the body just now; rather, He fashioned the body as dead from the very beginning. As I said, it is wicked by nature and a conspirator against the soul, though it does not appear so to all, but only to God, and to anyone who is a friend of God. For Scripture says, “Er was wicked before the Lord.” When the mind is occupied with heavenly things and is initiated into the mysteries of the Lord, it judges the body to be wicked and hostile; but when it departs from the investigation of divine matters, it considers the body to be a friend, a relative, and a brother. It therefore takes refuge in things friendly to the body. For this reason, the soul of an athlete and the soul of a philosopher differ. The athlete refers everything to the well-being of the body and would even sacrifice the soul itself for the sake of the body, since he is a lover of the body. But the philosopher, being a lover of the <term>kalon</term> <gloss>the noble or beautiful</gloss>, cares for that which lives within him—the soul—and disregards the body, which is dead, aiming only at ensuring that the best part, the soul, is not harmed by being bound to an evil and dead companion.

Four of the seven coverings are the passions, three are the various types of delusion and ignorance. Euagrius distinguishes them this way elsewhere. He speaks of the passions thus: "just as the knife circumcises the physical Jews, so the commandments of God circumcise the spiritual ones." Regarding the circumcision of ignorance, he says: "the stone knife is the teaching of Christ, which circumcises the reason, shrouded by passions, into true knowledge." There he speaks of the painful knife, here of stone, because purification from the passions is associated with more effort and pain than instruction, even though both are necessary for mutual perfection. Paul also teaches two types of circumcision. "You were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of flesh in the circumcision of Christ" (Col. 2:11). There he speaks of the circumcision of the passions. Regarding the circumcision of ignorance, he writes: "to this very day, when Moses is read, a veil lies upon their hearts; but when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed (II Cor. 3:15), and we are the circumcision who worship God in spirit (Phil. 3:3), and the circumcision of the heart (is what counts)" (Rom. 2:29). In the words "four of them are on the sixth day," the 6th day is a symbol of bodily labors, hardships, and the crucifixion; Israel worked six days and then rested. The fourth edition is very elaborate: containing all the books of Galen printed until now: better ordered than before, and more corrected than previously. It issues other books of his never before printed with the others: yet worthy of printing, decorating and perfecting his doctrine: to be newly printed in the third volume. At the end it is read: You have, most humane reader, this first volume of the works of Galen, a most illustrious teacher of the arts and medicine, corrected of very many errors: and purged of almost every fault (as much as was humanly possible): and produced in Pavia with the greatest care: by JACOB Paucidrapius of Burgofranco. In the year of our Lord 1515, on the day before the Kalends of October. The second volume was printed in Pavia, in the same year and by the same, on the Ides of October. The title of the third volume in the final part differs from the titles of the two previous volumes. — decorating and perfecting his doctrine: contained in this golden third volume most recently printed. At the end of this third volume these things are read: You have, most candid cultivators of sacred philosophy and medicine, in this third illustrious volume, various collected works of Galen, the monarch of physicians, clarified by various versions: and completed with the most exact care by the diligent man Jacob Paucidrapius: of Burgofranco: in PAVIA in the year from the virgin birth 1516. On the day before the Ides of June. fol. — This edition consists of three volumes. Rusticus Placentinus, a cultivator of medicine, oversaw the edition. He did not change the ancient versions, made from the Arabic, nor the more recent ones of Laurentius Laurentianus, Nic. Leonicenus, and Guil. Copus of the books of Galen.

Two sages, Rabbi Jose ben Kipar and the grandson of Zechariah ben Kabutal, were sent after him. He asked them, "Why have you come?" They replied, "We have come to study Torah." 

He began to proclaim before them: "These men are great sages, and they are the sons of great sages; their ancestors served in the Temple." <note>original: "שענו זכריה בן קבוטל"</note> Zechariah ben Kabutal mentioned one instance where a law seemed restrictive to him. He began to declare things ritually impure while they declared them pure; he prohibited while they permitted; he disqualified while they declared fit. 

He then began to proclaim about them: "These men are men of falsehood." They said to him: "You have already built, and you cannot demolish; you have already fenced, and you cannot break through. You declare things impure, but we declare them pure; you prohibit, but we permit; you disqualify, but we declare fit." They said to him: "And for what reason are you intercalating years and setting the new months outside of the Land?" He said to them: "Because..."

# Treatise on Astronomy, Chapter 16

<note>A faint astronomical diagram depicts several concentric circles and smaller orbs positioned along orbital paths, with lines connecting them to illustrate geometric relationships between planetary bodies.</note>

The mean conjunction <note>Hebrew: *molad*</note>, as I have already explained elsewhere, involves the wheel <note>Hebrew: *galgal*</note> that moves constantly to the west. There is the revolving wheel, the lesser wheel, and the zodiacal wheel. You will find that the wheel of the Moon is within the wheel of the Sun, and the wheel of the Sun is within the wheel of the zodiac. The wheel of Saturn is within them, for the zodiacal wheel revolves around the wheel of the Sun, and the wheel of the Sun revolves around the wheel of the Moon. It is also explained here, and in detail, that some appear fixed on the line of the eccentric wheel, and the exterior of the Sun is aligned and revolves opposite the line of the eccentric that divides it. 

The motion of the movement rotates across the entire circumference, fixed to the line of the eccentric of the small wheel, and the small wheel is fixed to the line of the eccentric. The line of the eccentric of the eccentric wheel tilts slightly from the line of the equinox of the zodiacal motion by a measure of five degrees. While it tilts, even when it lacks, it still revolves with its power during the movement. When it revolves, being a point of the circumference, the Sun is at point Z and point H. Thus, the true path of the Sun is the measure of the rotational movement of the eccentric wheel, and the mean path of the Moon is the measure of the rotational movement of the lunar wheel. Both of their eccentric wheels revolve from top to bottom for every cycle, which is the measure of the rotational movement of the small wheel revolving from east to west.

When the Sun and the Moon meet together, aligned one against the other, they exert force on the wheel at a single point, as if the Sun and the Moon were one rising point. This is called the conjunction of the Moon, and in the language of the astronomers, it is called the *kof* <gloss>conjunction/meeting</gloss> of the Moon. The explanation of the term *molad* <gloss>birth/conjunction</gloss> is that it is known the Sun illuminates the entire circuit of the wheels. It is similar to glass, which has no light of its own, but receives it. Thus it is with the Sun and all the stars, and the Moon as well, for all the light of the Moon is drawn to it from the Sun. 

The Sun and the Moon are like two round spheres, one within the other, and the sphere of the Sun is much larger than the sphere of the Moon. As it is in the wisdom of the stars, when two spheres are positioned against each other, the one receiving light from its companion is only illuminated to the measure of half the sphere that faces it. As one moves away from it, the Sun illuminates only the half that is directed toward its face, as explained to you in the Holy Zohar. When the Moon and the Sun of the solar wheel are positioned such that the sphere of the Sun and the sphere of the Moon are aligned, the time of the conjunction is during the day of the Sun’s obscurity. The half of the light is the lower part visible to us, while the other part of the Moon is dark and not visible. Above it is the Moon, and the light from the Sun is removed from it. Then, from the circuit of the movement, it is seen from the part of the movement that, by its power, it returns the light... <unclear>this matter settles the part and between the point of conjunction, for the light and the dark face the dark, it does not sit, it departs, and at every time the circumference is in its movement, a portion of the lunar wheel is for seven days, and then there is a complete cycle</unclear>.

# Treatise on Astronomy, Chapter 16

<note>A diagram depicts several concentric circles and smaller orbs, likely representing epicycles or celestial spheres in planetary alignment.</note>

The mean conjunction <term>molad</term> <gloss>birth/conjunction of the moon</gloss> is as already explained elsewhere, for the sphere moves westward constantly. The rotating sphere and the sphere of spheres is the <term>galgal ha-mazalot</term> <gloss>zodiacal sphere</gloss>. You will find that the <term>galgal ha-levanah</term> <gloss>sphere of the moon</gloss> is inside the <term>galgal ha-chamah</term> <gloss>sphere of the sun</gloss>, and the sun’s sphere is inside the zodiacal sphere, and the sphere of Saturn is within them. For the zodiacal sphere revolves around the sun’s sphere, and the sun’s sphere revolves around the moon’s sphere. It has also been explained here, and clearly, that some of them appear fixed on the axis of the <term>galgal ha-yotze</term> <gloss>eccentric sphere</gloss>, and outside the sun, it is aligned and rotates against the axis that divides it. 

The motion of the movement proceeds to every circumference fixed on the axis of the <term>galgal ha-ketanah</term> <gloss>minor sphere/epicycle</gloss>, and the minor sphere is fixed on the axis of the eccentric sphere. The axis of the eccentric sphere tilts slightly from the line of the zodiacal motion by an amount of five degrees. Although it tilts, even so, it rotates according to its power during the movement. Since it rotates so that the point of circumference and the sun are in the 17th and 18th chapters, the true motion of the sun is the measure of the rotational movement of the eccentric sphere, and the mean motion of the moon is the measure of the rotational movement of the lunar sphere. Their two eccentric spheres also rotate from above to below for every degree of movement, which is the measure of the rotational motion of the minor sphere, rotating from east to west. 

When the sun and the moon meet together, aligned one against the other—like a point—as if the sun and the moon were one single point of ascent and the like, this is called the <term>molad</term> <gloss>birth/conjunction of the moon</gloss>. Among the masters of astronomy, it is called the <term>kof ha-levanah</term> <gloss>lunar conjunction</gloss>. The explanation of the term <term>molad</term> is that it is known that the sun illuminates the entire circumference of the spheres, drawn and resembling it like glass which has no light of its own. Thus it is with the sun and all the stars and the moon too, for all the light of the moon is drawn to it from the sun. The sun and the moon are like two round spheres, one within the other, and the sphere of the sun is much larger than the sphere of the moon. As it is in the science of the heavens, when two spheres are one against the other, the one receiving light from its companion is not illuminated by more than the measure of half the sphere which faces it. The further one moves away from it, the more the sun illuminates in its presence, half the side which is aligned against its face. Just as is explained to you in the holy <term>Zohar</term> <gloss>foundational text of Kabbalah</gloss>, for when the moon and the sun of the solar sphere are in the solar sphere, and the sun and the half-moon are in the lunar sphere, the time of the <term>molad</term> serves in the day of the sun’s darkness, and half the light is the lower part visible to us, and the moon’s part is dark and invisible. Above it is the moon, and the light from the sun is removed from it. Then, from the circumference of the motion, it appears from the division of the motion by its power... <unclear>this matter is settled in part and point of the molad, for when light is against light, it is not settled in part and moves, and at every time of the circumference in its movement, a part of the lunar sphere is toward the seventh day, and then there is a complete conjunction</unclear>.

If the path is one, why are there many paths? Or why does it branch into many divisions or incline toward many matters? Does it desire to travel a road or a path, or are the trails narrow and short while the paths are long, and the roads broad? The trails and the paths are among the nations <note>likely referring to the differentiated realms of created beings</note>, while the roads are engraved in the image of male and female, and the matter of the affair spreads and becomes intertwined in wondrous miracles. From these wonders, a flame <term>Shalhevet</term> <gloss>flame</gloss> emerges. From the flames that go out, threads become thick and strengthen in the eye until they become princes. This is the principle: everything returns in a cycle, blending and moving until it reaches the dwelling of the heavens, which are called three hundred and ninety firmaments. These are the residence of the Holy One, blessed be He. This is before the creation of the mist, the <term>Hashmal</term> <gloss>radiance/electrum</gloss>, the curtain, the throne, the angel, the seraph, the <term>Ofan</term> <gloss>wheel (a type of angel)</gloss>, the <term>Hayyah</term> <gloss>living creature</gloss>, and the multitudes <note>in another version it is written: star</note> and the four, which is a square from which they emerged. This was before the creation of the seas, springs, lakes, rivers, and streams, and before the creation of the living creatures, cattle, birds, fish, swarming things, reptiles, humans, princes, harmful spirits, Lilith, and all kinds of light. There was the light which is the essence, from which emerged the light surrounded by thousands of thousands of myriads of lights. This is the primordial light, which is the essence; for this reason, it is called the Holy Spirit. 

Know the path, for before these things that we have mentioned, there was nothing there but the air we spoke of. It was a darkness from two matters. From these types of sources, this air flowed, and the sparks that went out—the number of the springs was fast, like sparks going out all at once, dispersing into many parts like when a craftsman strikes with a hammer. After this, one spring was drawn, from which darkness was drawn. The darkness is like a kind of color: one is the darkness like the dawn, which is like green; one is a darkness that is mixed with green and blue; and one is a white darkness mixed with green, blue, and red. This is the primordial darkness that went out from the air. Do not worry about investigating it or the matter of its investigation, for even Moses our teacher could not ask about it; that is to say, not even a question, and certainly not an investigation. Everything he said was only so that the knowledge of the image of the Holy One, blessed be He, would not change within them. When the knowledge was before him as one, that is, when the matter was clarified in the heart, he knew the correct knowledge and it was set in his mind, even though he did not have to investigate or watch for a higher degree than this and demand it when he already knew and recognized with complete intent and not lack of intent. Concerning this, he said, "Show me now Your ways," and the Holy One, blessed be He, answered him, "You will not be able to see My face," meaning this darkness whose knowledge you seek, which was the source for all from me and my origin, you will not be able to stand upon the clarification of its investigation. About this, He said, "And you will see My back, but My face will not be seen." This means you will not be able to attain it so that you might say of Me, as one says of others, "So-and-so is from such-and-such a place and source, and such-and-such is from such-and-such a place." Of this, you cannot know the knowledge of this darkness that is set in its existence, but from here on, you will know everything. That is, from this darkness downward, you will know even the creation of My own self and the greatness of My name and My glory. At that moment, Moses began to look at the primordial air, which is the essence as we have said, and he found it to be darkness from two matters, from two sources. The first flows and the second flows. The prophecies were drawn through the pipes and the vessels, and the labor returns to be thus, like dew. The <unclear>baskets</unclear> return to be only more, until it returns into thin, fine threads, and is led and drawn until they are finished drop by drop, fine and small. Those drops combine and become pieces, and the pieces go and grow until they are drawn and come out with great strength, drawing near to one another, mixing with one another, spreading and joining until moistures come out from them. The moisture drips and is drawn and congeals, and in the congealing it becomes clear, whitened, and clarified until those first pieces that we mentioned separate, and from them emerges a kind of foam that floats on the surface of the water and becomes everything. And from the moistures, spirit emerges, and this is the Holy Spirit. Concerning this, it is said, "And the spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters," meaning the spirit was strengthening in holiness and was made into chambers upon chambers, and every chamber was made into a branch, and every branch was made into a root by itself, from which many matters and many things go out. Here you have the clear words and the allusions so that you may know and understand the Holy Spirit.

If it is a path, and it is a path; and if it is one path, is it divided into many, or into several parts, or does it incline toward several matters? Does one desire to go by way of a road or a path? Are the trails narrow and short, the paths abundant, the roads wide? The trails and paths are among the nations, and the roads are engraved in the likeness of male and female, and the essence of the matter spreads and blossoms in wonders of wonders. I have wondered at its wonders, and from the wonders [came] the flame, and from the flames that go out and go out, the threads thicken, strengthening in their source until they became princes. This is the main point: that everything returns in a cycle, circulating and going up to the peak of the supernal heavens, which are called three hundred and ninety firmaments. These are the dwelling place of the <term>HaKadosh Baruch Hu</term> <gloss>the Holy One, Blessed be He</gloss>. Before they were made—mist, lightning, the curtain, the throne, angel, seraph, ophanim, living creatures, and the multitude (in another version it is written: also star) and <unclear>rabi'a</unclear>, which is the square from which it emerged—before the days, the springs, the pools, the rivers, and the streams were created, and before the creation of the beasts, cattle, birds, fish, creeping things, living things, man, princes, and harmful spirits, Lilith, and all kinds of light, there was a light that is the essence. From it emerged the light that is surrounded by thousands upon thousands of myriads of <unclear>myriads</unclear> of lights. This is the primordial light, which is the essence, and for this reason, it is called the Holy Spirit. 

You must know the path, for before these things that we have mentioned, there was nothing there but the air we spoke of. It was dark from two aspects of kinds of sources from which this air would flow, and the sparks that emerged—the number of emanations was rapid, like sparks that emerge all at once, scattering into several parts at the moment the craftsman strikes with a hammer. After it follows the one source from which the darkness is drawn, and the darkness is a kind of color. One is the darkness like the break of dawn, which is like green; one is dark, and it is mixed with green and azure; and one is white darkness mixed with green, azure, and red. This is the primordial darkness that emerged from the air. Do not trouble yourself to investigate it or the matter of investigating it, for even <term>Moshe Rabbeinu</term> <gloss>Moses our teacher</gloss> could not ask about it—that is, he could not even pose a question, let alone an investigation. Everything he said was only so that the knowledge of the image of the Holy One, Blessed be He, would not change within them. When the knowledge was before Him as one—that is, when the matter was clarified in the heart, that he knew the true knowledge, and it was directed in his mind—even though he did not have to investigate and expect a higher degree than this, and to inquire into it when he would know and recognize with complete intention and not directed—regarding this he said: "Show me now Your ways." The Holy One, Blessed be He, replied to him: "You will not be able to see My face," meaning: this darkness, the knowledge of which you seek, which was everything from Me and My source, you will not be able to arrive at the clarification of its investigation. Regarding this He said: "And you will see My back, but My face shall not be seen," meaning: you will not be able to attain it so that you might say, "Because I am like other others, I will say 'so-and-so' is a seraph from such-and-such a place, and the source of so-and-so is from such-and-such a place." Regarding this, you will not be able to know the knowledge of this darkness, which is directed in its existence. But from here on, you will know everything. That is, from this darkness downward, you will know even the creation of My own self, the greatness of My name, and My glory. 

At that moment, Moses began to look into the primordial air, which is the essence, as we have said, and he found it dark from two aspects, from two sources. The first flows and the second flows, and the emanations were drawn through the conduits and channels, and the flow returns to be thus, like dew, and the streams return to be [so], only with an increase, until it turns into thin threads. It behaves and is drawn until it ends in drops—thin, small drops. Those drops combine and become pieces, and the pieces go and grow until they are drawn and emerge with great strength. They approach one another, mix with one another, spread, and combine until moisture emerges from them. The moisture drips, is drawn, and congeals. Upon congealing, it becomes clear, whitened, and purified until those first pieces we mentioned are separated. From them emerges a kind of foam, which floats upon the face of the waters, and everything becomes moist. From that moisture, spirit emerges, and this is the Holy Spirit. Regarding this it is said: "And the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters," meaning the spirit was strengthening in holiness and was made into chambers, chambers. Every chamber and chamber became a branch, and every branch and branch became a root in its own right, from which several matters and several things emerge. Here you have the clear things and the hints so that you might know and understand the Holy Spirit.

The judges. The son shall stand in place of the father. Those who are involved, we assess for them according to their obligations. For a debt owed to a woman <note>referring to her marriage settlement</note>, it is paid from average-quality land, and for a woman's marriage contract, it is paid from the poorest-quality land. Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Bun said: Explain the matter according to everyone in the case of a <term>diatheke</term> <gloss>will/testament</gloss>. He brought forth the matter, we understand regarding oaths on the claim of a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor; but here, even though we do take oaths against a minor or for the Temple treasury, we collect from the property of a minor, and we collect from a person [even] when he is not present. Rabbi Yirmiah said: Explain it in a case where she is eating from it, and the court collects the house. Explain it in a case where he is a guarantor for him who is appointed.

Likhsa said before Rabbi Mana: We act according to how you do [it]. We send <term>diatigmatin</term> <gloss>official court summons/edicts</gloss>; if he comes, that is good, and if he does not come, we confiscate his property. He said to him: We also act this way. We proclaim for thirty days; if he comes, that is good, and if not, we confiscate his property. He said to him: Imagine yourself [in a case] where he is in a distant place. He said to him: We send three letters, one within thirty days, and one within thirty days, and one within thirty days; if he comes, that is good, and if not, we confiscate his property. Rabbi Hanina said: And he stood in judgment, but the person did not speak in judgment; we do not confiscate, and we do not proclaim. You might find that Hanan and Rabbi Shimon both said the same thing. Just as you say the law follows Hanan, so too the law follows Rabbi Shimon. Rav said: If the borrower died, the lender takes an oath to the heirs, and even if the lender died, the heirs of the lender take an oath to the borrower. But if the borrower died first and then the lender, the lender has already become obligated to the children of the borrower to take an oath, and a person does not bequeath his oath to his children. Rabbi Yochanan heard this and said: Let that man eat and rejoice. Rav Hiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav [said] a document...

The judges shall stand, the son in place of the father. Those who are seized <note>referring to claimants or creditors</note> are appraised for their liens, and for the debt of a wife, it is from the intermediate <term>beinonit</term> <gloss>land of medium quality</gloss>, and for a wife's marriage contract, it is from the poorest <term>zibburit</term> <gloss>land of inferior quality</gloss>. Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Bun said: Explain this according to all parties as referring to that specific legacy <term>diateki</term> <gloss>will/testament</gloss>. Bring [the case of] the master, we shall understand regarding oaths on the claim of a deaf person, an imbecile, or a minor. But here, they say one does take an oath to a minor and to the Temple treasury. They collect from the property of a minor. And they collect from a person who is not present. Rabbi Yirmeyah said: Explain it as referring to one whose field is being eaten by him, and the court collects the house. Explain it as one for whom a guarantor was appointed. Liksa said before Rabbi Mana: We perform the matter of "where are you?" We send <term>diatigmata</term> <gloss>official court summons/edicts</gloss>; if he comes, that is good, and if he does not come, we confiscate his property. He said to him: We also do this; we proclaim for thirty days, if he comes, that is good, and if not, we confiscate his property. He said to him: Imagine for yourself that he was in a distant place. He said to him: We send three letters, one within thirty days, and one within thirty days, and one within thirty days; if he comes, that is good, and if not, we confiscate his property. Rabbi Chanina said: And [only if he] stood in judgment, but if a person did not stand in judgment, we do not confiscate and we do not proclaim. You might find it said: Chanan and Rabbi Shimon, both said the same thing, just as you say the law follows Chanan, likewise the law follows Rabbi Shimon. Rav said: If the borrower died, the lender takes an oath to the heirs, and even if the lender died, the heirs of the lender take an oath to the borrower. But if the borrower died first and then the lender, the lender has already become obligated to the heirs of the borrower for an oath, and a person cannot bequeath his oath to his sons. Rabbi Yochanan heard and said: Let that man eat and rejoice. Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav: A bond...

### Mareh HaPanim

**Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Bun says:** That is to say, since he said a minor is like an adult, this refers to a minor orphan. As I have written inside, since it is not like that in [Tractate] Ketubot and Gittin, and all of them were corrupted in the print, missing [text] from hereafter. I have already explained in Gittin there that the claim of... it is difficult for the teacher, why should they give, they are appraised regarding an adult, and this is its language, to say [even] minors, whether for inferior land or for intermediate land. For that which is written regarding inferior land, there is a dispute among the authorities at the end of... in the name of... like Rabbi Yehuda. It can be said that [the law] suffices for them regarding the creditor, for he does not set his mind upon the orphans, and the property fell before the orphans... regarding the law of the Torah, regarding inferior land for minors, we make a regulation for them, for adults, and such is the opinion of Rambam, may his memory be for a blessing, there. And the anonymous language of the words of Rambam, may his memory be for a blessing... it seems so... and he wrote... that even from the... before it comes to his hand, by the hand of the orphans... and they collect to the body from the inferior land. And I wrote there that one should not bring proof from the discussion here according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Yitzchak, may his memory be for a blessing, for it is implied from the discussion that he holds that even regarding a creditor, they differ between an adult orphan and a minor orphan, for it is established, that is to say, [the phrase] "the son shall stand in place of the father," etc., all of them [refer] to an adult orphan specifically. And it cannot be said that the Talmud holds that [the term] "orphan" returns to... that even regarding a creditor they differ regarding intermediate land, as it is there in [Tractate] Bava Metzia... as I explained in Yoma there, that the dispute is [regarding] a creditor in intermediate land, and it is resolved well [as] an adult... and it requires examination.

**Explain it:** as one for whom a guarantor was appointed. See in Chapter Chazakat, furthermore the law in [Tractate]... it will be explained for this, appointed from his name, and he explained there that he was invalidated from this...

**Liksa said before Rabbi Mana:** Apparently, one can learn from here regarding the matter of receiving testimony not in the presence of the litigant, according to the opinion of the teacher... and not all [testimony] that is received not in his presence... and all the colleagues say there is no... and we confiscate his property, for the law is that it can be explained that Rabbi Chanina concludes, "and stood in judgment," etc., and if so, they have already received the testimony in his presence while standing in judgment, and we require the warning of the property... in his presence before it is dealt with here, and upon this he concludes that we do not confiscate immediately... for we do not proclaim at the beginning, and so it is in the first chapter of [Tractate]... and see above in this chapter... law 8... regarding the matter of receiving testimony not in the presence of the litigant... and from this one can learn that... before he stood in judgment, for in such a case they receive testimony not in his presence, as he says that we proclaim, and afterwards...

**And likewise:** the law follows Rabbi Shimon. I have already written regarding this in Ketubot... that which is explained there that... as Chanan... and concerning that which was explained as... that the Mishna is divided, the seller conditioned, the seller, etc., and he is exempt from the oath, and he holds that he does not hold so, [therefore] the law is not like Rabbi Shimon.

**Rabbi Yochanan heard:** and said, "Let that man eat and rejoice." Rabbi Yochanan, who holds like Rabbi Shimon, that if the lender died, this oath is [extinguished]... and it has already been clarified...

I intend to write here a portion of the introduction to <term>Alfasi</term> <gloss>a prominent medieval rabbinic authority, Rabbi Isaac Alfasi</gloss>, and therein I will also clarify some matters of faith, as they appear to my humble opinion, according to the limitations of my intellect and my meager understanding, and as a remembrance of days gone by.

At the beginning of my words, I wish to make known some of the foundations of religion and faith according to the path I have observed in his ways. For all complete paths are those upon which they stood, and through them, one perceives the wisdom, ethics, discernment, and intellect of the preceding generations. Also, in this, I will explain to you the words of our sages <term>Ḥazal</term> <gloss>our Sages, of blessed memory</gloss> in their homiletical teachings and the stories found in the Talmud. Each and every one of these matters deserves to be known and understood according to the truth within them, not according to their literal appearance. Otherwise, someone might think or understand these matters according to their simple, literal meaning, or the simple interpretation of the statements, which is not possible according to abstract reason, nor according to true judgment. It is certainly good to find the proper interpretation of these aforementioned matters, for these are the essence of the Torah and the commandments.

The Rabbi <note>referring to Alfasi</note> also said in his introduction to the tractate <term>Berakhot</term> <gloss>Blessings</gloss>, and these are his words: "And this is what is written, 'On the Sabbath day, keep it holy to the Lord, for in six days the Lord made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh day He rested and was refreshed.'" The Rabbi, of blessed memory, wrote: "Behold, the scripture makes it appear as if the Holy One, blessed be He, rested on the seventh day, etc. In truth, this is not the case, for the Almighty, blessed be He, does not attain weariness or fatigue, nor, Heaven forbid, does He require rest and refreshment. Rather, everything is by way of parable and metaphor, according to our limited comprehension and intelligence." This is the subject referred to in the Torah, and it is written therein in many places, for we have seen the words of our Sages in their homiletics and statements that indicate things that appear strange in their literal sense. Yet their explanation and their inner meaning are profound, and they are true matters concerning the paths of faith and rational truths. It is fitting for us to acknowledge and understand these matters with our intellect, lest our words be as those who speak in mockery, Heaven forbid. What is good for a person to see is that he should study the interpretations and the books that explain these matters according to sound reason. Behold, such words have come down in the scripture; the one who understands will understand. All these things are the words of the living God.

The famous wise man, the author of <term>Akedat Yitzhak</term> <gloss>Binding of Isaac, a philosophical commentary on the Torah</gloss>, of blessed memory, also wrote in the first gate that everything depends on the understanding mind. Thus, the words of our Sages are to be interpreted in many places, for Heaven forbid that they would write things that have no taste or scent, God forbid.

He concluded: May the Holy One, blessed be He, in His abundant mercy, show us the path of truth, and teach us Torah and knowledge, and place in our hearts discernment and intellect to understand, study, and teach, and to keep and perform all the words of His Torah in truth and integrity. Amen, Selah. This is what I wished to mention here regarding the matter of some of the words of our Sages, the homileticians, and regarding the matter of faith, as mentioned previously.

My intention is to write here a portion of the introduction to <term>Alfasi</term> <gloss>a reference to the Halakhic compendium by Rabbi Isaac Alfasi</gloss>, and in it, I shall also explain some matters concerning faith according to what appears to my humble opinion, within the limits of my short-sightedness and meager understanding, remembering the days of old.

At the beginning of my words, I wish to make known some of the foundations of religion and faith according to the path I have observed in their ways. For all the complete paths are the paths upon which they stand; in them are revealed the knowledge, ethics, understanding, and intellect of the previous generations. In this, I will also clarify for you the words of our Sages in their homilies <term>derashot</term> <gloss>exegetical interpretations</gloss> and the narratives found in the <term>Talmud</term> <gloss>the central text of Rabbinic Judaism</gloss>. Every single one of these matters is worthy of being known and understood according to their inner truth, not according to what is apparent from them. Otherwise, one who thinks or understands these matters according to their literal sense—and the literal meaning of the statements which are not possible according to abstract reason nor according to true judgment—might err. What is certainly good is to find the interpretation of these mentioned matters, for these are the essence of the <term>Torah</term> <gloss>the Five Books of Moses/Law</gloss> and the <term>mitzvot</term> <gloss>commandments</gloss>.

The Rabbi also said in his introduction to <term>Berakhot</term> <gloss>the first tractate of the Talmud</gloss>, and I quote: "This is what is written, 'On the Sabbath day, it is holy to the Lord, for in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day He rested and was refreshed.'" The Rabbi, of blessed memory, wrote: "Behold, the scripture suggests that the Holy One, blessed be He, as it were, rested on the seventh day, etc. In truth, the law is not so, for the Blessed Name does not attain weariness nor exhaustion, and God forbid that He should need rest and refreshment. Rather, everything is by way of metaphor and analogy, according to our limited comprehension and knowledge."

This is the matter called by the <term>Torah</term> <gloss>Law</gloss>, and it is written within it. We have seen in many places the words of our Sages in their homilies and in their statements that point to things that appear strange in their literal reading, while their explanation and their inner meaning are deep and true matters regarding the paths of faith and the intellect. It is proper for us to recognize and understand these things with our intellect, lest our words be like those who mock, God forbid. What is good for a person to see is that he should study the interpretations and the books that explain these matters according to sound reason. Behold, such things have come into the scripture, and the one who understands will understand. All these things are the words of the living God. 

The famous sage, the author of the <term>Akedah</term> <gloss>a philosophical-homiletical work by Isaac Arama</gloss>, of blessed memory, also wrote in the first gate that everything depends on the intellect of the one who understands. Thus, the words of our Sages are interpreted in many places, for God forbid that they should write things that have no taste or scent, God forbid. He concluded: "May the Blessed Name, in His abundant mercy, show us the way of truth and teach us Torah and knowledge, and place in our hearts understanding and intellect to comprehend, learn, teach, observe, and perform all the words of His Torah in truth and sincerity. Amen, Selah." 

This is what I wanted to mention here regarding some of the words of our Sages, the homilists, and regarding the matter of faith as stated previously.
