### Regimen of maturatives
Warmth is of such a nature that it conforms to the natural warmth of the body, creating a certain <term>inviscatio</term> <gloss>process of making viscous or sticky</gloss>. Among these, in the first degrees, is a poultice with warm water and an application of wheat flour or barley, and masticated wheat is honey. Into this is placed bread with pitch or wax and saffron and powdered frankincense and pitch with oil of roses, or pork fat, or a poultice of mallow, orris, and linseed. And again, a poultice of sweet, fatty, and rich figs, or with barley flour, and barley flour again, and especially if hyssop or wild oregano is placed in it, or if it is mixed with water in which they are boiled with a little salt, not excessive. And sometimes fat or oil is placed in it, or two parts of glue of whites <note>egg whites</note>. And medicines composed of <term>vivum</term> <gloss>arsenic sulfide/orpiment</gloss>, <term>vorax</term> <gloss>borax</gloss>, galbanum, myrrh, laudanum, resin, butter, mastic, hyssop, <term>buida</term> <gloss>perhaps a variant of "buia" or wild rue</gloss>, root of donkey cucumber, and root of dragon's blood. And the poultice of Galen with oil of castor without wax, and especially when this poultice is dissolved in oil, it becomes the <term>didimoa</term> <gloss>a medicinal plaster</gloss> and the <term>basilicon</term> <gloss>a royal plaster</gloss>. And among the good things for this is the medicine from the stone <term>marchasite</term> <gloss>pyrite or iron sulfide</gloss> with ammonia, which is placed on top until it falls off by itself.

### Regimen of those that are breaking when they are mature. L. XXIX
When you find an abscess with thick skin, for which you do not expect it to burst on its own, and there are veins, tendons, and nerves there, then it is necessary that you incise it, because if you leave the <term>saniem</term> <gloss>sanious or thin, watery discharge</gloss>, it will rot, corrupt, and corrode the skin and the filaments of the nerves. That will indeed be more severe when it is near joints, and you should seek the location of the <term>saniem</term> with your incision. And be careful that the incision hole falls lower, unless it is not possible, and if that which is above the abscess is thick and you have cut, then cut only the hole, and when you apply the plaster, include the part behind it, and if it has been thinned, then cut its entire length. And know that the place where the <term>saniem</term> is, is declared by touch, and when you touch it with a finger, especially watch with the other fingers of the other hand whether anything is expelled from it. And the location of the <term>saniem</term> indeed appears from the deviation of the color toward whiteness, and when it is mature, it deviates toward redness. And sometimes the place of the <term>saniem</term> is inclined toward redness and yellowness when the <term>saniem</term> is not good, to be sensed by touch without sight, although sight assists. It is necessary, therefore, that in the incision you follow the natural lines of the skin, which are along the fibers, unless there is necessity, and in limbs diversified by the position of the fibers in length and in the place of the incision. For if you follow that in the incision of an abscess that is above the forehead, the incision will cause the skin of the forehead to fall over the face; rather, it is necessary that you diversify the incision. In those that are like the groin, it is necessary that you go with the incision in the width of the skin. And when you have incised the abscess and extracted what is in it, now it is necessary that you help to glue the skin to the flesh so that it does not tear and harden and become such that it does not glue, whereby it becomes a <term>sinus</term> <gloss>a hollow cavity or fistula</gloss> that does not cease to be filled and drains from the threads of the first abscess. And if it is necessary for you to use it, introduce a probe, on the head of which is rough cloth with which you cleanse the inner parts, then make it adhere and preserve it with a binding as we shall say about the bindings of cavities and ulcers; it will be very suitable. And it is necessary that you observe in the incision that which we said about the conditions, where you incise in a more mature place and a part farther away from veins, arteries, and tendons.

<column-break/>

Antyllus says if the abscess is in the head, then its incision is made wide, and if it happens in the nose, we shall incise it equal to the size of the length of the nose. And if it is near the eye, we shall incise it with an incision the shape of the head of a new moon and make the tortuosity downward. But if it happens in the jaw, we shall cut it with an equal incision, when the composition of this place is equal, and that is known from the bodies of the <term>fenu</term> <gloss>the senses or natural dispositions</gloss>. Behind the ear, however, we incise it; all these we incise in length. He says if it is near the hips, we shall incise it with a round incision, and a round incision is indeed that which captures with its grip the length of the body and some of its width. He says when this place is not incised roundly, it is possible that the matter gathers in it and they become <term>fistulae</term> <gloss>tubular ulcers</gloss>. And it is also incised that which is near the anus, because of the place of moisture that gathers in it. And in the side and ribs, it is incised by opening, but in the testicle and penis, in an equal manner. He says we should always be ready so that the incision follows the figure of the place as much as we can upon it. The sides and the auxiliaries are cut in length, and preserve so that you do not injure the nerves. And know that the incision is diversified according to the locations, for when it is the eye, then its longitudinal incision is wide according to the position of the eye, and in the nose it is with the length of the nose, and in the jaw it is with the length of the jaw, and near the ear it is cut equally when the position of this place is equal, and that is known from the bodies of the senses. Behind the ear, however, it is incised equally, in the arms, legs, thigh, and penis it is all made equally in length, and it is made in the muscles and in the back; in the groins and the lower abdomen, you shall place the incision to take from the width also, lest a <term>sinus</term> <gloss>cavity</gloss> be made in it that becomes a <term>fistula</term>. And likewise in that which is near the anus, take from the width also lest a <term>sinus</term> arrives and it becomes a <term>fistula</term>. And the testicles and penis equally and in length; in the side and ribs take in the width also so that it is transverse, as the position of the ribs is made and the flesh that is upon them. He says consider always the position of the flesh and the fibers of the muscles, for they are not prepared together except for this, that we may incise with the imitation of the place so that it does not arrive at an inclusion and the place of the <term>incarnatio</term> <gloss>healing/fleshing over</gloss> becomes good, not thick. And in everything, dispose your study so that you do not cut an artery, nor a large vein, nor a nerve, nor the fibers of the muscle, and the incision is made according to the size of the abscess. But if it is small and that which is in it runs from one place, then cut it in one place; and if it is large, then incise it from the beginning, then introduce your left index finger into it and incise it where the head arrives, and then introduce it also into the opening, and according to this until you arrive at the top of it. And if the abscess has a sufficient place from which it is possible for that which is in it to come out, we shall incise it in that place. And if it is round or has a figure so that what is in it does not come out with one incision, we shall incise it in the inner part of itself in two or three places, according to the quantity that you know, for everything that gathers in it runs in an hour. He says, let there be no abscess in a puncture, or a noble member, or a member near a bone, or in danger, we shall hasten in the incision, and sometimes we confirm its maturation lest it corrupt any of these members. I say, therefore, that this is the regimen when we find no excuse for incision. But if we hope that it breaks through, we shall not incise, and similarly if we hope that it bursts through medicines causing eruption; perhaps, indeed, we find in medicines causing eruption that which stands in the place of an incision. And many times the skin is incised with some incision or something is taken from it, afterward, eruptions are placed upon it so that it may have its incision.

D'EBN-KHALDOUN.

The situation is like that of rays and light, which, when emitted from centers, spread in circles across the surface of water when it is struck. When these circles encounter old age and weakness, they begin to diminish from the edges, while the center remains preserved until God decrees the total extinction of the matter. At that moment, the center itself is extinguished. If a state is overcome from its center, the survival of its peripheral regions and borders is of no use, and it collapses immediately. The center is like the heart from which the spirit emanates; if the heart is overcome and seized, all the limbs are defeated. Consider this in the case of the Persian state, for its center was <term>al-Mada'in</term> <gloss>Ctesiphon</gloss>. When the Muslims conquered <term>al-Mada'in</term>, the rule of Persia collapsed entirely, and it did not help <term>Yazdgard</term> <gloss>the last Sassanid King</gloss> that he still held the peripheral regions of his kingdom. 

The opposite is true of the Roman <note>Byzantine</note> state in Syria. When its center was Constantinople and the Muslims conquered Syria from them, the Romans withdrew to their centers in Constantinople. The loss of Syria from their hands did not harm them, and their rule remained connected to the center until God decreed its extinction. Consider also the condition of the Arabs at the beginning of Islam, when their tribal unity was abundant, and Egypt was conquered in the fastest time. Then, they moved beyond that to the lands of Sindh, Abyssinia, Ifriqiya, and the Maghreb, and then to Andalusia. When they dispersed into portions across the kingdoms and frontier regions, settled as garrisons, and their numbers were exhausted by these distributions, they ceased their further conquests, and the expansion of Islam stopped.

<summary>Ibn Khaldun explains the theory of the state center by comparing it to the heart of an organism, using the fall of the Persian Empire and the resilience of the Byzantine Empire to illustrate why a central power is essential for the survival of a realm.</summary>

# Guai <note>original: "夬" (Hexagram 43, representing "Breakthrough" or "Resolution")</note>

Proclaimed in the king’s court. Sincere calls for action involve danger. Proclaim it from your own city. It is not advantageous to take up arms. It is advantageous to have a destination to go to.

## Tuan Zhuan <note>original: "彖傳" (Commentary on the Judgments)</note>

Guai means to break through. It is the firm breaking through the yielding. It is creative and joyful; it is decisive yet harmonious. "Proclaimed in the king’s court" signifies that one yielding line is riding upon five firm lines <note>referring to the configuration of the hexagram where the top line is yin and the five lines below it are yang</note>. "Sincere calls for action involve danger" signifies that the danger will manifest in a way that leads to brilliance. "Proclaim it from your own city; it is not advantageous to take up arms" signifies that relying on force leads to exhaustion. "It is advantageous to have a destination to go to" signifies that when the firm grows and prevails, the end is reached.

Kong Zhongda says: The king's court is the place where the hundred officials are located. The superior man resolves against the petty man, and therefore he can clearly proclaim his decision. This demonstrates complete impartiality without secret bias. If one only uses prestige and violence, or treats this as taking up arms, then one is simply valuing force to achieve victory. This is being decisive without being harmonious, and thus the way becomes exhausted.

Wang Jiefu says: The yielding line rides upon five firm lines. The top-six line rides upon the firm line of the nine-five, and the multitude of yang lines are close to the five, personally deciding on the five.

## Tuan Zhuan (Commentary on the Judgments)
Guai means to decide. The strong decides against the yielding. Being vigorous and joyful, the decision is harmonious. "Announced in the king’s court" because the yielding one <note>the yin line at the top</note> rides upon five strong ones. "Sincere calls, there is danger," for such danger brings brilliance. The noble person decides against the petty person, so one can openly proclaim and make the decision. This demonstrates complete impartiality without secret bias. If one relies solely on force and severity to take up arms, this is merely valuing strength to achieve victory. This is a case of deciding without harmony, and such a path will eventually lead to exhaustion.

Wang Jiefu <note>Wang Anshi, 1021–1086 CE, a Song dynasty statesman and philosopher</note> says: The yielding one rides upon five strong ones. The top-six line rides upon the strength of the nine-five line. The multitude of yang lines are close to the fifth position, personally deciding [the fate of] the fifth.

# Containing beauty, one may be persevering; if one follows the king's affairs, one achieves a glorious result

The number two occupies the earth position, which correctly aligns with the foundational position of Heaven and Earth. The Heaven hexagram <note>Qian</note> is centered on the nine-in-the-fifth position; therefore, the fifth line discusses the great application of Heaven, while the nine-in-the-second position only speaks of the beauty of Heaven's virtue. The Earth hexagram <note>Kun</note> is centered on the six-in-the-second position; therefore, the second line discusses the great application of Earth, while the six-in-the-fifth position only speaks of the beauty of Earth's virtue. The "straightness" of the six-in-the-second line is precisely the ability to be extremely yielding and yet move with firmness. The "squareness" of the six-in-the-second line is precisely the state of being extremely still while the virtue remains square. Its "greatness" is the result of acting as a follower who eventually becomes a leader, maintaining constancy, containing all things, and transforming them with brilliance. The phrase "without special effort, there is nothing that is not advantageous" describes the way of Earth: it follows Heaven and acts according to the times. The six-in-the-second line fully embodies the virtue of Earth. Confucius feared that people would not understand how the six-in-the-second line could possess the straightness of Heaven, so he explained it by saying, "The movement of the six-in-the-second line is straight and square." This refers to the movement of Earth. It is the firmness of the interior that allows for this straightness. He also feared that people would not understand why the six-in-the-second line is always advantageous, so he explained it by saying, "The way of the earth is glorious." This means that the way of the earth is centered on the six-in-the-second line, just as the way of Heaven is centered on the nine-in-the-fifth line. It is positioned to embody the virtue of Heaven. ○ Cai Qing says: The way of the earth is straight and square. Its brilliance consists of being straight, square, and vast. By dwelling in that which is straight, square, and vast, one naturally finds nothing that is not advantageous. ○ Ye Ershan says: View the word "straight" in relation to "square." The movement of the six-in-the-second line is square, but this is because what is preserved within is straight. It is because of this internal straightness that what is manifested externally is square.

# Containing inner beauty and remaining steadfast, one may act according to the times. To follow the king’s affairs means to know that the light is vast.

The number two in the earthly lines correctly aligns with the fundamental positions of <term>Qian</term> <gloss>the Creative</gloss> and <term>Kun</term> <gloss>the Receptive</gloss>. <term>Qian</term> is centered on the nine-five position, which is why it speaks of the great application of <term>Qian</term> at the fifth line, while the nine-two line only speaks of the beauty of <term>Qian</term>’s virtue. <term>Kun</term> is centered on the six-two position, which is why it speaks of the great application of <term>Kun</term> at the second line, while the six-five line only speaks of the beauty of <term>Kun</term>’s virtue. The "straightness" of the six-two line is the manifestation of supreme softness moving into firmness. The "squareness" of the six-two line is the manifestation of supreme stillness possessing square virtue. Its "greatness" is the manifestation of being a follower who becomes a leader with constancy, containing the myriad things and transforming them with vast light. Its "no need to practice, yet nothing is disadvantageous" is the manifestation of the way of <term>Kun</term>, following heaven and acting in accordance with time. The six-two line truly possesses the complete virtue of <term>Kun</term>. Confucius feared that people might not understand how the six-two line could concurrently possess the straightness of <term>Qian</term>, so he explained it by saying: the movement of the six-two line is straight and square. This means that when <term>Kun</term> moves, it is firm, and that is how it can be straight. He also feared people might not understand why the six-two line is "nothing disadvantageous," so he explained it by saying: the way of the earth is vast. This means the way of the earth is centered on the six-two line, just as <term>Qian</term> is centered on the nine-five line; it occupies the position of heavenly virtue.

○ Ye Erzhans says: Interpret "straight and square" as one concept. The movement of the six-two line is square, yet it originates from the straightness stored within. It is because of this internal straightness that it manifests as squareness on the outside.

When one does not impose [on others], there is a distinction between that which requires effort and that which is effortless. The practice of <term>shu</term> <gloss>reciprocity</gloss> also contains differences between sincerity and a lack thereof; one cannot simply claim that there remains a barrier of selfish intent. When one does not impose upon others what one does not desire for oneself through force of will, this is not natural reciprocity, and it still falls short of sincerity. When one does not impose upon others because one naturally refuses to do so, this is the reciprocity of natural, true sincerity. Yet, this has not yet reached the level of <term>ren</term> <gloss>humaneness/benevolence</gloss>. 

I have already distinguished the difference between <term>ren</term> and <term>shu</term> in my two chapters on the <term>Lunyu</term> <gloss>Analects of Confucius</gloss> passages: "Do not impose upon others what you do not desire yourself," which can be called the method of <term>ren</term>. Reciprocity is only capable of extending the refusal of what one does not desire—that which is not good—so that it does not reach others; it has not yet reached the stage of extending what is good to others. Advancing one step further, one extends what one desires for oneself to others, just as in the principle of "caring for one’s own elderly and extending that care to the elderly of others."

# Chapter VII.

->Pharaoh’s hardening by his wise men / and the first plague of the land.<-

AND the Lord said to Moses: See / I have set you as a (a) God to Pharaoh / and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet! <margin>(a) Ps. 82/6.</margin>
2. You shall speak everything that I shall command you: but Aaron your brother shall speak it to Pharaoh, that he may let the children of Israel go out of his land.
3. But I (a) will harden Pharaoh’s heart, that I may do many of my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt. <margin>(a) c. 4/21. c. 8/15. c. 10/27. Rom. 9/17.</margin>

4. And Pharaoh will not listen to you, that I may set my hand against Egypt, and lead my hosts, my people, the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt through great judgments.
5. And the Egyptians shall know that I am the Lord, when I stretch out my hand over Egypt, and bring out the children of Israel from among them.
6. Then Moses and Aaron did as the Lord commanded them; so they did.
7. And Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three years old, when they spoke to Pharaoh.
8. And the Lord spoke to Moses and to Aaron and said:
9. When Pharaoh shall speak to you and say; Show a miracle for yourselves! then you shall say to Aaron: Take your staff and cast it before Pharaoh, that it may become a dragon.

<margin>Since kings wish to recognize no one as their superior except God and the sword, they must accept how God wills to exercise this supreme authority over them, directly or through others.</margin>
Moses was here to appear as a messenger from God, both to present God’s command to Pharaoh, and—should he prove disobedient—to threaten him with God’s judgments and actually carry them out upon him. All those in power should take this to heart and bow under the mighty hand of God when He lets His command be presented to them through His servants, whose spirit they could examine if they would be humble and recognize the justice of the cause that God demands of them.

v. 1. **I have set you as a God to Pharaoh)** That is: You good man, you fear him now, but he shall fear you as if you were his God! I will impress such a secret awe upon him. Therefore, Moses often told him the hard truth to his face thereafter.

Annihilated souls are like the gods of princes. For when everything that is of the creature has vanished from them, nothing can remain but God alone. The interpreters of such annihilated people are their prophets: since they preach nothing but the words of God, when they bring forth for the benefit of others that which these souls, who have become God through the total annihilation of themselves, express.

**Prophet)** Prophets here are those who present the word revealed by God to others to whom God wishes to make His will known. God gives the former the spirit of revelation, and the latter the gift of eloquence, and [the necessity] that they must recognize the finger of God in the former, and thus accept it for God’s sake. See Chap. 4/15, 16. See also an example of this in Ananias and Saul, Acts 9/10, 20.

v. 3. **I will harden Pharaoh’s heart)** That is: I will accomplish nothing with Pharaoh through all these miracles but the hardening of his heart; so that his heart will not be softened by them, but rather hardened further.

God has a great wealth of goodness and long-suffering: but when a man, little by little, has collected a great treasure of evil for himself through the deceit of sins, and has grown strong in wickedness; then the judgment of hardening comes upon him, so that God departs from him and withdraws His grace: after which withdrawal the man falls from one sin into another, from one evil into another. And God can certainly do this through righteous judgment. Thus Pharaoh hardens himself, and is hardened, or his own hardening is, as it were, sealed by the Lord.

Paul probably best understood how it is said of God that He hardens the heart, when he exclaimed: Do you despise the wealth of the goodness, patience, and long-suffering of God? Do you not know that God’s patience seeks to lead and move you to repentance? But you, because of your stubbornness and your impenitent heart, heap up wrath for yourself against the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God! Rom. 2/4, 5.

Because the Lord does not punish Pharaoh in his own person or his close relatives [immediately], it is said by the Lord, because of this goodness and gentleness, that He hardens his heart: whereas otherwise Pharaoh has actually hardened his own heart more and more through the opportunity that God spared him; until the death of his firstborn son awakened him. For then he began to give way, and his hard heart became more yielding: because he feared he would now have to be the next.

<column-break/>

<margin>v. 7. It is a thoughtful division in the life-age of Moses. He spent 40 years in his court life, where he was raised according to the manner of the great and wise of the world: he had to spend 40 years in a foreign land in Midian in a simple way of life, and therein, as it were, forget the vanities of the world and its sciences: and for 40 years he led the people in the wilderness, and managed the difficult office of regent among them.</margin>
Thus, souls must first be weaned from all earthly things and let themselves be emptied of them in silence, until they can be deemed worthy of a greater grace and divine revelation.

v. 9. The unbelievers demand signs and miracles, and God gives them the same: but experience teaches how little these affect perverse souls: on the contrary, such people believe more in lying powers, signs, and wonders; whereby they only allow themselves to persist and harden in their error and injustice, as also happened here. See 1 Cor. 14/22; 2 Thess. 2/9, 10.

However, this miracle should teach all regents that if they make the regent's staff and scepter entrusted to them by God into a rod of the wicked and a scepter of rulers—that is, in harshness—then God will surely break it at the right time, with which they strike the peoples in fury without ceasing and rule with rage over the nations, Isa. 14/5, 6; yes, with which they also become burdensome to the lot of the righteous, Ps. 125/3. But this staff will also become a dragon for them, and, insofar as they have accepted the power of the dragon, the old serpent, and exercised its cruelty, so shall they also share in its lot, Rev. 13/4, 12. They should therefore rather learn to wield the love-scepter of the kingdom of the Lamb in mercy, kindness, justice, and wisdom, for a blessing upon themselves, their descendants, and their subjects and lands.

Aberrations of the intellect are therefore the source of evil;

aberrations of the will the source of falsehood;

aberrations of actions the source of ugliness and disharmony.

Our intellect takes part in the first; our heart in the second; our action in the third, when we think, will, or act outside of unity.

These considerations lead me further to the recognition of human purpose, which must necessarily consist in elevating ourselves to unity and, with it, forming a whole once more.

Since we observe that evil, falsehood, deformity, and irregularity exist in the world, man must necessarily have abandoned his purpose and, as a consequence, fallen into error through the intellect, into illicit desire through the heart, and into vice through actions.

The first spirit that separated its intellect from the order of unity was necessarily the source and origin of evil.

The heart that took part in this error was the first to corrupt its will, which caused the first separation, in which we still feel the consequences of the aberration.

Hence proceed those contrary effects which are breathed out by winds, whether they are opposed in location and condition, or by nature suited to the universal sublunary element. From this, both concord and discord, along with a multiform variety of meteors, are produced within it. Hence arises the multiplicity of affections, the opposition of dispositions, the passions of spirits, and, to use one word, that sympathy and antipathy which is observed to exist among creatures, both simple and composite, whether they be animal, vegetable, or mineral. The author, therefore, stimulated by these foundations, concludes that it is fair and just to subscribe to the opinions of those two most excellent philosophers, Heraclitus and Empedocles, regarding this matter. One of their opinions is that all things are made through strife and enmity, that is, from enmity and friendship; the other is that the soul is composed of the four elements and of friendship and strife. Arguing from this, he addresses that contrary disposition which exists between the watery spirit or the humid nature of the world and the clear ray of the luminous mind, in respect of their origins. For, by strife, he understands both spiritual and bodily contention, in respect, namely, of that contrary power or strength which exists between the formal and all-informing light and the dark matter, as much by reason of the body in the act of corruption, when the soul is prepared to depart from it, as in the antipathetic or irascible passion with respect to the soul, in which the spirit labors and suffers preternaturally. And these opinions of the aforementioned philosophers do not seem to differ from the sense of the wise man who says that God has made all things double, one contrary to the other, and nothing has been made which is deficient.

->CHAPTER I.<-

->In this chapter it is demonstrated that God is that pure, most simple, and universal unity which comprehends within itself all number and multitude.<-

Just as there is no one, however exalted in the sphere of mathematical perfection or deeply immersed in the mystical entrails of abstruse arithmetic, who, with the agile intuition of his more mature intellect, can observe or discern any thing that might deservedly claim a place before unity in either order or antiquity (whence unity is recognized by the wisest of philosophers to be the principle and root of all numbers and multitude), so indeed no one consistent with himself can deny that this radical identity, as it is considered in its pure and simple nature, cannot be limited by any quantitative dimension, or included or comprehended in any number, or divided into distinct portions, or defined by any substance or entity. And hence it is concluded by the wise that unity is the most ancient and most radical principle of all things, as it is that which comprehends within itself all substances, quantities, and qualities, not otherwise than a point in geometry, considered in its bare and simple essence, is observed to be indivisible, being indeed something barely perceptible and as it were nothing determinable; and yet, the point is recognized by mathematicians
<column-break/>
to be the infallible root, not only of any geometric line but also of all other dimensions continuous in mathematics and physics, inasmuch as it comprehends all magnitudes within itself and is comprehended by none.

Thus, experienced mathematicians have found two principles of all dimensions whatsoever, in that they preceded and excelled all other things in the nature of things in order and time, in imitation or image of the most interior, most central, and most abstruse point in the divinity, or of the most splendid unity remaining in the same state in which it existed before the creation of the world, namely, when it reserved itself, hidden and secret within itself, that is, from every act of creation. So that in this condition of the existence of unity, it could not be held as God, insofar as it had not yet produced any creature by creation from which it might be worshipped as God; nor could it be rightly held as Father, since it did not yet appear to have begotten any son, whether archetypal or typical; nor did it seem to be estimated as the supreme good, insofar as the abyss, still buried in darkness or deformed <term>hyle</term> <gloss>prime matter</gloss>, did not yet participate in its luminous and vivifying goodness: for, as yet

->§. XV.<-

<margin>Marmots.</margin>
On the very highest Alps, and in such places where no trees grow and only a little pasture exists, at least for sheep, and where they can often be grazed in the summer for up to six or even eight weeks, one finds animals that are somewhat larger than rabbits, which are called <term>Murmel-Thiere</term> <gloss>marmots</gloss> (<term>Marmottes</term>). Their color is a mixture of gray and reddish, their flesh is good to eat, and in taste it is almost like pork. They can whistle very loudly, and they are accustomed to sleeping in their burrows for eight to nine months of the year, for as long as these mountains are covered with snow. Indeed, they sleep so soundly then that if they are pulled out of their holes at such a time by those who know their burrows, one cannot wake them up except through great heat or very hot water. When they go out into the field in the summer, they generally stay together in groups, where one always has to stand sentry on a high point and give a signal to the others by whistling as soon as any danger is present, whereupon they retreat back into their holes as quickly as possible.

<margin>Euestra <note>Paracelsian spirits</note> do not perform miracles.</margin>
That the <term>Euestra</term> <gloss>spirits or specters described by Paracelsus</gloss>, as he calls them, lack the power of miracles is known by itself. They are nothing other than shadows, or demons, or household gods and spirits of the Platonists, that is, true devils; we have shown most firmly above that they cannot perform miracles. If they seem to perform something at any time, they either accomplish this by joining agents to patients or by applying female substances, or they deceive and cast shadows before the eyes in place of real things, or things that God does through them by some divine counsel are thought to have been done by them. It remains, therefore, that we first declare that the power of that faith of which he speaks, that is, imagination, is not what he, along with certain others, has ignorantly, foolishly, and impiously thought it to be. Next, we must show that not even through <term>magia</term> <gloss>magic</gloss>, and its various forms, can anything of this kind be accomplished. Finally, if we have leisure and the matter seems to demand it, we shall add something about the efficacy of the heavens and prophecy, and thus we shall bring the first part of our skirmish to an end, unless perhaps something occurs in the meantime that requires explanation. FUR. The plan is entirely pleasing. Nor do I desire that it be demonstrated to me at length that in herbs, stones, and medicines which we usefully employ to drive away diseases, there does not reside the power to produce miracles. "In whatever is purified in dreams,

By that very wisdom of the Victorious One,
One shall be victorious over Mara <note>the personification of delusion and death</note>."

He spoke. Then, the Tathagata Vajra-phala-dāna <note>original: "rdo rje phal cher sbyin"</note> entered into the meditative absorption called the "Vajra Emitting Radiance of the Play of the Lotus, the Secret of All Buddhas," and recited this heart of enlightenment:

"The peaceful dharani, the seat of the appearance of all,
Adorned by this jewel,
Showing the truth in a mere moment,
It becomes the ground of the wisdom essence."

He spoke. Then, the Tathagata Śāntamati <note>original: "zhi ba'i blo gros"</note> entered into the meditative absorption called the "Vajra that Sets Forth All Realms of All Buddhas Without Exception," and recited this heart of enlightenment:

"From the ocean of Victorious Ones, the gathering of clouds,
Virtuous in all three times,
The pure land is the body of wisdom light,
All phenomena arise from the appearance of the mind."

He spoke. Then, the Victorious Vajrapani, the Lord of Secrets, the Blessed One, commanded the innate excellence to be attained through the conduct of wisdom: "Just as the unresiding space is pervasive..."
